definition: Irreversible means impossible to undo or turn back.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word irreversible. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know irreversible should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Extinction is irreversible: no funding, apology, or breeding program calls back a species whose last member has died.
A lasting change endures on its own, but nothing stops a determined effort from unmaking it; irreversible is the change no effort touches.
Ingrained habits are worked deep into the grain — hard, slow work to undo, but people undo them every day; irreversible ends the argument: there is no undoing at all.

Irreparable belongs to damaged things: harm that no repair can undo — the cracked bell, the burned fresco, the broken trust. Irreversible belongs to processes and changes — a reaction, a decline, a decision's effects that cannot run backward. The fire's damage was irreparable; the burning itself was irreversible.

Unalterable means no one can modify a thing — the treaty's wording, the trust's terms — whether or not anything has happened to it yet. Irreversible is narrower and points backward: something has already changed or begun, and no power can now run it the other way.

You can start over with new sugar, but this batch is one-way.
Irreversible says something stronger than lasting or drastic: the road back does not exist.
A lasting change endures but might, at great cost, be unmade; an irreversible one has no unmaking at any price.
The word draws a one-way arrow on time itself.
Irreversible is for processes and changes — damage, reactions, ecological one-way doors.
Its close unit-mate irrevocable is for commitments: a promise, gift, or ruling that its maker cannot call back.
The wetland's draining is irreversible; the deed that allowed it was irrevocable.
And reversible, their shared opposite, is the door that still swings.

Ferry pilots crossing the Pacific mark a point on every chart called equal-time — the moment when turning back and pressing on cost the same fuel.
Before it, a bad forecast can still send you home.
After it, the choice to continue is, in a strict sense, irreversible: no maneuver returns you to the runway you left with the fuel you have.
Instructors are careful with the word.
The flight is not doomed after the point, they say — only committed.
Everything else stays adjustable: altitude, speed, even the destination airfield can change to meet the weather.
What cannot change is the direction of the journey itself.
From that line onward, the only way out is through.
